extracted.intended_audience: chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, SDS and label preparers, occupational safety and health professionals, hazard classifiers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and final-rule decisions from OSHA on updating the Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) classification and labeling criteria to align with GHS Rev. 7 (and selected Rev. 8 items) across multiple physical hazard chapters (pyrophoric gases, aerosols, gases under pressure, flammable liquids, oxidizing gases, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Note 4 — classification threshold for pyrophoric gas mixtures (absence of data)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of data on its pyrophoricity, a flammable gas mixture should be classified as a pyrophoric gas if it contains more than 1% (by volume) of pyrophoric component(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA agreed with commenters that the wording should be mandatory and is finalizing the provision by changing “should” to mandatory language (“shall be”). Cal/OSHA requested lowering the threshold to 0.01% and making testing mandatory; OSHA declined because GHS subject-matter expert text (1%) was used and HCS does not mandate testing. The 1% threshold triggers mandatory classification only when no test data are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of test methods and consensus standards for flammable/pyrophoric gases
rubrics_metrics.description: Update references to consensus standards and test methods (e.g., ISO 10156:2017, ISO 817:2014, IEC 60079-20-1, DIN 51794, UN Manual of Tests and Criteria Part III) for classification of flammable gases and pyrophoric/chemically unstable gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA proposed and finalizes updating the cited consensus standards and test methods in B.2.3.1 and adding guidance paragraphs B.2.3.2–B.2.3.4 describing test methods for pyrophoricity and chemical stability. These references indicate acceptable methods for determining hazards but do not themselves create a testing mandate under the HCS.

rubrics_metrics.name: When testing is optional and the role of experience/expert judgment (B.2.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where test data are not available, classifiers may use experience or expert judgment to determine whether to apply classification procedures for pyrophoric gases, except that test data, when available, supersede experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explained B.2.3.3 allows classification using experience for mixtures with less than 1% pyrophoric component in the absence of testing; it does not permit experience to override existing test data. Cal/OSHA argued this gives undue discretion; OSHA disagreed and retained the paragraph, noting the constraint that mixtures ≥1% must be classified as pyrophoric when no test data exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCS does not mandate testing (general policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA does not require testing under the Hazard Communication Standard; SDS and label preparers must use all available data and relevant experience when classifying chemicals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated clarification that including references to test methods or standards in the HCS describes acceptable approaches — not a requirement that manufacturers/importers/distributors perform testing themselves. OSHA has long held this position (citing prior Federal Register statements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of updated ISO/consensus methods to new vs. already-classified chemicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Updates to reference standards and test methods apply to new chemicals or chemicals not already classified using an earlier version of the standard; OSHA is not requiring reevaluation of chemicals already classified under an earlier ISO 10156.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA will not force reclassification of materials already classified with earlier test-method editions; the updated criteria are prospective for newly classified chemicals or those not previously classified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosols — addition of non-flammable aerosol Category 3
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt Rev. 7 criteria to add a non-flammable aerosols Category 3: aerosols that contain ≤1% flammable components (by mass) and have a heat of combustion <20 kJ/g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA determined adding Category 3 better captures hazards of non-flammable aerosols and avoids mislabeling aerosols as compressed gases. The Category 3 definition is applied in Table B.3.1; OSHA aligns with Rev. 7 decision logic for aerosols rather than adopting the Rev. 8 table text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosols should not be cross-classified as gases under pressure or flammable liquids
rubrics_metrics.description: Aerosols (flammable and non-flammable) should not also be classified as gases under pressure or flammable liquids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explained that aerosol containers differ from pressurized gas cylinders in container characteristics and failure mechanisms; to avoid over-warning and confusion, aerosols will generally be excluded from simultaneous classification as gases under pressure or flammable liquids, and OSHA is adding notes to Appendix B.3 and B.6 to that effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerosol decision logic and Category 3 interpretation (Rev. 7 alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Rev. 7 decision logic: Category 3 applies when the chemical does not meet the criteria for Categories 1 and 2 and (1) the chemical contains <1% flammable components (by mass) and (2) has a heat of combustion <20 kJ/g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarified wording/format to avoid confusion (adding numbered subclauses for Category 3) and declined to adopt Rev. 8 table language because of potential inconsistencies; OSHA will review Rev. 8 at the UN subcommittee level before adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on compressed gas cylinder pictogram for aerosols
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA will not allow the optional use of the compressed gas cylinder pictogram on aerosol labels (non-flammable or flammable aerosols are not to bear the compressed gas pictogram).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA found optional pictogram use would cause inconsistency and 'over warning' and could dilute messages for compressed gases. OSHA noted an exception: aerosol cans already released for shipment as of the labeling compliance date need not be relabeled and may bear the compressed gas pictogram.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of 'chemicals under pressure' hazard classification (Rev. 8 item)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is adding 'chemicals under pressure' as a hazard classification within Appendix B.3, including definitions, classification criteria (three categories per Rev. 8 Table 2.3.3), and hazard communication elements (per Rev. 8 Table 2.3.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA places chemicals under pressure within the aerosols chapter (renaming B.3 to 'Aerosols and Chemicals Under Pressure') rather than as a separate chapter; it will provide separate definitions, criteria, and communication elements to distinguish the hazards and avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gases under pressure — definition measured at standard conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 'gases under pressure' to read: 'gases which are contained in a receptacle at a pressure of 200 kPa (29 psi) (gauge) or more at 20 °C (68 °F), or which are liquefied or liquefied and refrigerated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA added the 20 °C (68 °F) reference to clarify that the pressure of the receptacle is measured at a standard temperature. OSHA also added a note to Table B.5.1 clarifying that aerosols should not be classified as gases under pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flammable liquids — footnote for boiling point and storage determination (Footnote 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the appropriate flammable liquid storage container size and type, the boiling point shall be determined by §1910.106(a)(5). The manufacturer, importer, and distributor shall clearly note in Sections 7 and 9 of the SDS if an alternate calculation was used for storage purposes and the classification for storage differs from the classification listed in Section 2 of the SDS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarified that the §1910.106 accommodation (e.g., using the 10% distillation point per ASTM D-86 for mixtures without a constant boiling point) is an accepted method for storage determination in specific circumstances and does not change HCS classification. If an alternate calculation changes the storage classification relative to Section 2, the alternate calculation and the differing storage classification must be documented on the SDS (example note: 'Initial boiling point 80 °F/estimated boiling point 100 °F (for storage purposes)'). This requirement is informational and not a testing mandate; acceptable methods are identified but testing is not required by HCS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oxidizing gases — reference the most recent ISO 10156 edition
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise the note in B.4.1 and text in B.4.3 to clarify that provisions refer to the most recent version of ISO 10156 for definition and classification of oxidizing gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is finalizing this clarifying update; as with other updates, it applies to new chemicals or chemicals not already classified and no comments were received opposing the change.
